name: Fela Kuti
tagline: The man who turned music into a weapon against tyranny
story:
In 1977, Lagos was a city of contradictions — gleaming wealth for the few, crushing poverty for the many. Fela Anikulapo Kuti, already Nigeria's most dangerous musician, had built the Kalakuta Republic, a commune that was part recording studio, part free clinic, part living protest. His Afrobeat anthems didn't just make people dance — they named names, called out corrupt generals, and gave voice to millions who had none. The military government had tried bribes, threats, and arrests. Nothing worked. Fela kept playing.

Then came February 18th. A thousand soldiers stormed Kalakuta. They beat everyone inside — men, women, children. They threw Fela's 82-year-old mother from a second-floor window; she would die from her injuries months later. They burned the compound to the ground. They destroyed his recordings, his instruments, everything. When asked who was responsible, the military said the damage was caused by "an unknown soldier."

Fela's response was to write an album called Unknown Soldier. He rebuilt Kalakuta. He ran for president. He married 27 women in a single ceremony partly as a political statement against colonial marriage laws. He was arrested over 200 times. And he never, not once, stopped playing. Every night at his club, The Shrine, songs stretched past 20 minutes — sprawling, furious, joyful compositions that were equal parts concert, sermon, and revolution.

They could burn his house. They could break his bones. They could kill his mother. But they could never silence the music. Fela proved that art isn't a luxury — it's the last thing tyrants can take from you, and the first thing that outlives them.
